title: Thermally quenched metastability in metal-insulator transitions via elemental substitution
authors: Hiroshi Oike, Yasunori Takahashi, Keisuke Shibuya, Masaki Nakano, Tatsuki Hanada, Motoaki Hirayama, Hiroko Tokoro, Fumitaka Kagawa
abstract: Thermal quenching inhibits equilibration toward the thermodynamic ground state during phase transitions, revealing metastable phases such as structural glasses and quenched alloys. Whether such thermally quenched metastability can be realized in metal-insulator transitions has remained an open question because these transformations are governed by collective electronic reorganization rather than atomic diffusion. We demonstrate that rapid cooling exceeding 10$^9$ K s$^{-1}$ kinetically avoids the metal-insulator transition, stabilizing a long-lived metastable metallic phase in tungsten-substituted VO$_2$. Temperature-dependent relaxation reveals nucleation-dominated kinetics with a thermal activation barrier introduced by tungsten substitution. Our results establish elemental substitution as a route to thermally quenched metastability in metal-insulator transitions, expanding metastable phase control to electronic phases.
summary: This paper demonstrates that elemental substitution can induce thermally quenched metastability in metal-insulator transitions, moving the concept beyond purely structural systems. By rapidly cooling $	ext{V}_{1-x}	ext{W}_x	ext{O}_2$, the authors stabilize a long-lived metallic phase that relaxes back to the insulating state, confirming that electronic reorganization can be kinetically trapped.
main_problem: The study investigates whether thermally quenched metastability, typically seen in structural glasses, can be realized in metal-insulator transitions (MITs) governed by electronic reorganization.
main_result: Elemental substitution in $	ext{V}_{1-x}	ext{W}_x	ext{O}_2$ successfully stabilizes a long-lived, metastable metallic phase upon rapid cooling, confirming that electronic phases can exhibit quenched metastability.
method: The research combines ultrafast laser quenching experiments with detailed kinetic modeling (Arrhenius analysis) and theoretical frameworks like the Slichter–Drickamer model and phase-field simulations.
model_or_system: The primary system is tungsten-substituted vanadium dioxide ($	ext{V}_{1-x}	ext{W}_x	ext{O}_2$). The theoretical modeling uses concepts from phase transitions, free-energy landscapes, and domain evolution kinetics.
key_observables: Metastable metallic phase persistence, relaxation time ($	au$), activation barrier ($\Delta$), and the equilibrium site fraction ($\alpha$).
important_parameters: Quenching rates exceeding $10^9 	ext{ K s}^{-1}$; activation barriers in the range of $500–700 	ext{ K}$; doping concentration $x$ in the range $0.05–0.15$.
main_assumptions: The kinetics are modeled as being nucleation-dominated, and the analysis relies on the assumption that local structural variations induced by substitution create the necessary energy barriers.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the temperature-composition phase diagram showing the metastable region, time evolution of resistance post-quenching, and real-space optical imaging confirming nucleation-dominated relaxation.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the physical feasibility of quenching MITs to detailing the experimental evidence in $	ext{V}_{1-x}	ext{W}_x	ext{O}_2$, followed by detailed kinetic modeling using free-energy theory and phase-field simulations to explain the microscopic origin of the metastability.
why_interesting: The work bridges concepts from structural glass physics (quenched metastability) into electronic phase transitions, providing a framework for controlling electronic states via non-equilibrium thermal protocols, which has parallels in controlling quantum states.
